title: The Scotch Game
description: The Scotch is one of the oldest openings in chess, dating back to the year 1750. It also was Levy's first ever chess opening! It's easy to learn and the ideas are quite fun.

r1b1k1nr/p1pp1ppp/1p3q2/2b5/4P3/2N1Q3/PP.text:
Black attacks our queen, the bishop being supported by the b6-pawn.

We'll move the queen to the side. On g3 it is placed well, since it doesn't interfere with our minor piece development.

r1b1k1nr/ppp2ppp/1b1p1q2/8/4P3/2PB4/PP2Q.text:
Black fights for the e5-square.

Since our queenside is yet to be developed, we'll get our king into safety by castling kingside.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1ppp/1b3q2/8/4P3/2PBQ3/PP3P.text:
Black attacks our queen.

We'll retreat to e2, the safest square for our queen. Here the queen also defends f2.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1ppp/5q2/8/1b2P3/4Q3/PPP2PP.text:
Black develops with check.

We'll block with the pawn, gaining a tempo on the bishop.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1ppp/5q2/b7/4P3/2P1Q3/PP3PP.text:
Black retreats to a5.

We'll develop the bishop to d3 from where it supports the e4-pawn.

r1b1k2r/ppp1nppp/1b1p1q2/8/4P3/2PB4/PP2Q.text:
Black wants to castle as well.

We want to develop the queenside minor pieces quickly! Having played c3 on move seven, we no longer have c3 for our knight.

r1b1kb1r/ppppqppp/5n2/4P3/3Q4/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
Black defends the knight by pinning the e-pawn.

We'll interfere the pin with the bishop, after which the knight on f6 is under renewed attack.

r1b1kbnr/p1pp1ppp/1p3q2/8/4P3/4Q3/PPP2PP.text:
With ...b6 Black aims to quickly develop the bishop pair.

We'll develop our knight, aiming at the d5-square.

r1b1kbnr/ppp1qppp/3p4/4P3/3Q4/2N1B3/PPP2.text:
Black challenges our strong e5-pawn.

But we'll centralize the knight and attack the queen.

r1b1kbnr/ppp2ppp/3q4/3N4/3Q1B2/8/PPP2PPP.text:
...but this allows Bf4!

We are attacking the queen, and the pawn on c7 behind it, which will fall next.

White is completely winning.

r1b1kbnr/ppp2ppp/3q4/3N4/3Q4/4B3/PPP2PPP.text: Black recaptured with the queen to avoid Bb5, which would have won the queen owing to the fork on c7...

r1b1kbnr/pppp1ppp/5q2/8/3QP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
This is the engine's top choice and the second most popular move, played in almost 20% of the games.

We don't want to trade the queens, as it would help Black with their development.

r1b1kbnr/ppppqppp/8/4P3/3Q4/4B3/PPP2PPP/.text:
Black retreats.

We'll develop our queen's knight. d5 looks like a great square for it!

r1b1kbnr/pppq1ppp/3p4/3NP3/3Q4/4B3/PPP2P.text:
Black moves their queen to d7.

Black's king is uncastled, so opening up the center is a great idea, and we'll take on d6.

r1b2rk1/ppp1nppp/1b1p1q2/8/2N1P3/2PB4/PP.text:
Nc4 aims to win the bishop pair.

Once we capture the bishop on b6, we can push f4 to gain more space on the kingside and use the bishop pair to our advantage!

r1bq1rk1/pp1pbp1p/1n4p1/2p1P3/4QB2/2NB4/.text:
After castling queenside our position is very comfortable.

We have more space, better developed pieces and better control over the center. 

We can start to improve our pieces with Rhe1, Nd5, and Bh6.
Black prevents the mate by blocking the battery.

r1bq1rk1/pp1pbppp/1n6/2p1P3/4QB2/2N5/PPP.text:
Black hides their king.

But we can develop a piece with a checkmate threat.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1bppp/3p1n2/8/3QPB2/2N2P2/PP.text:
And with the move f3, we support the pawn on e4 and prepare a kingside attack with g4 and h4! 

Kb1 is also a useful move in many positions where we've castled queenside.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1bppp/3p1n2/8/3QPB2/2N5/PPP2.text: Black also gets their king out of the center and into safety.

r1bqk2r/pp1pbppp/1n6/2p1P3/4Q3/2N5/PPP2P.text:
Black prepares to castle.

Now Bf4 reinforces the pawn on e5, aims at the weakened d6-square and prepares to castle queenside!

r1bqk2r/ppp1bppp/3p1n2/8/3QPB2/2N5/PPP2P.text:
Black prepares to castle short.

We'll get the king into safety and centralize the rook by castling queenside.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/1n6/2p1P3/4Q3/8/PPP2PP.text:
Black retreats to b6.

We'll develop. Our knight aims at the weak b5 and d5 squares.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/5n2/2p1P3/3Q4/8/PPP2PP.text:
Black attacks our queen instead of retreating the knight, which occurs in around 20% of the time.

We bring the queen to e3 so that ...Qe7 doesn't pin the e-pawn and simply loses the knight.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/8/2p1P3/1n2Q3/8/PPP2PP.text:
Black brings the knight to b4, intending to retreat to c6 in the future.

We just develop the knight, aiming at weak light squares in the black camp.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/8/2pnP3/8/4Q3/PPP2PPP/.text:
Black attacks our queen.

We'll bring it to e4, attacking the knight in return.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/8/2ppP3/1n2Q3/2N5/PPP2PP.text:
Black expands and attacks our queen.

But we can capture en passant, with discovered check!

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/8/3QP3/2N5/PPP2PP.text:
Black develops their knight.

By developing the bishop to f4 we add control over the e5-square and prepare to castle queenside.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/8/3QP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Black goes for the third most popular move 5...Nf6, which is a mistake!

It allows us to immediately attack the knight with e5.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/8/3QP3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.text:
And Black goes for the most popular move, 5...d6 played in almost 40% of the games. 

Black opens up the light-squared bishop and most importantly, fights for the e5-square.

We'll develop the knight, fighting for central squares.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
Black develops and protects e5.

Now 3.d4 is the signature move of the Scotch! We go for central activity.

3.d4 immediately creates two threats: capturing the pawn on e5 or pushing d5 with a tempo, gaining central space.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
Black trades on d4.

This happens in nearly 90% of the games, as other moves are inferior.

We'll recapture with the knight.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/3nP3/8/PPP2PPP/RNB.text:
Black trades again, not allowing us to double their c-pawns.

This trade is the most popular move under 2000. Played nearly 45% of the time, the problem with it is that our queen arrives rapidly in the center of the board.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/3Pb3/1Bp5/1n2Q3/2N5/PPP2P.text:
Check! And Black's position collapses shortly. 

They'll have to retreat the knight to c6, where it is attacked twice.

r3k1nr/pbp2ppp/1p1p1q2/2b5/4PB2/2N3Q1/PP.text: Now we get our king into safety on the queenside. We'll aim to continue developing with Bb5+ and also push e5 to open up the center.

r3k1nr/pbpp1ppp/1p3q2/2b5/4P3/2N3Q1/PPP2.text:
Black fianchettoes.

We'll develop our bishop with an attack on the c7-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black goes for ...e5.

We'll bring the knight to f3 as is usually done in e4-e5 openings.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the first chapter of the Scotch! 

The Scotch is a great opening choice for e4 players who want to avoid the Ruy Lopez or the Italian Game. 

Our opponent opts for ...e5 and ...Nc6, but we immediately spice things up in the center with d4 and often get an active, tactical position!

Let's get into it, starting with 1.e4!

2kr3r/pppbnppp/2np1q2/2b5/1PBNP3/2P1B3/P.text:
Our plan is pretty straightforward: a queenside pawn storm!

We will play a4 and b5. 

It also comes with tempi on Black's minor pieces.

3r1rk1/ppp2ppp/2n1q3/2p1P3/5P2/2P5/PP1N2.text:
Black pins our knight to the queen.

So we'll unpin with Qc2.

3r1rk1/ppp3pp/2n1qP2/2p5/5P2/2P5/PPQN2PP.text:
We'll trade since the pawn would be lost otherwise.

The f-pawn provides some spatial advantage on the kingside and allows for a potential future attack.

We have ideas of Nf3 or Ne4. 

The a-rook will side to e1 to gain control over the e-file.

3r1rk1/ppp3pp/2n1qp2/2p1P3/5P2/2P5/PPQN2.text: By playing ...f6, Black challenges our central pawns.

r1b1k1nr/1ppp1ppp/1p6/4P3/8/8/PPP2PPP/RN.text:
Black recaptures, opening the a-file for their rook.

Our knight comes out. The d5-square looks great!

We also clear the way for castling.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1ppp/1q6/4P3/3Q4/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
Black offers a queen trade yet again.

Now we'll recapture. 

Black must damage their pawn structure and our pawn provides some spatial advantage for the endgame.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1ppp/2n2q2/2b5/3NP3/4B3/PPP.text:
By moving the queen to f6, Black adds an attacker to the knight on d4. Alternatively, 5...Bb6 6.Nf5 is promising for us.

We can add support to our central knight by playing c3.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1ppp/5q2/8/3QP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
...so they offer a queen trade.

We'll decline, and attack the queen in return.

Trading on f6 would also help Black develop the knight.

r1b1k2r/1pppnppp/1p6/4P3/8/2N5/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Black prevents us from jumping into d5.

By castling queenside we get our king into safety and also bring the rook into the game.

r1b1k2r/ppp1nppp/2np1q2/2b5/2BNP3/2P1B3/.text:
In 20% of the games, Black continues with ...d6.

They are opening up the c8-bishop for development, and protecting the other bishop on c5.

We'll get the king into safety.

r1b1k2r/ppp1nppp/3b1q2/1N2n3/4p3/2P1B3/P.text:
Black covers it.

We'll set up a small trap with Bc5.

Black cannot trade due to checkmate.

r1b1k2r/ppp1nppp/3p1q2/2b1n3/3NP3/2P1B3/.text:
Black could go for 8...d6, which occurs 20% of the time.

We'll simply castle and get our king out of the center.

r1b1k2r/ppp1nppp/5q2/2b1n3/3Np3/2P1B3/PP.text:
Black grabs the "free" pawn, which was played in 70% of the games!

Now Nb5 actually threatens a checkmate with Nxc7+ and Qd8#!

r1b1k2r/ppp1nppp/5q2/2bpn3/3NP3/2P1B3/PP.text:
24% of games continue with Black striking in the center with ...d4, posing a question to our pawn on e4.

We'll get the king into safety, sacrificing the pawn on e4 but in return, we'll get ahead in development.

r1b1k2r/ppppNppp/8/8/2B1P3/2P1b3/PP3PqP/.text:
...but we grab the knight on e7!

White has won a piece here.

r1b1k2r/ppppnppp/1q6/2b1n2B/3N4/2P1B3/PP.text:
Black creates a queen-bishop battery, which occurs almost 20% of the time.

We'll immediately attack the bishop with b4.

r1b1k2r/ppppnppp/1q6/4n2B/1P1b4/2P1B3/P2.text:
Black trades.

Now we'll recapture with the bishop, hitting the knight on e5 and attacking the queen.

r1b1k2r/ppppnppp/2N5/2b5/2B1P3/2P1B3/PP3.text:
Black creates a threat against our rook...

...so we'll bring it to f1 and now  Black's bishop on c5 is hanging!

r1b1k2r/ppppnppp/2N5/8/2B1P3/2P1b3/PP3Pq.text: Black tries to avoid losing material.

r1b1k2r/ppppnppp/2n2q2/2b5/3NP3/2P1B3/PP.text:
Black develops the knight to e7 and prepares to castle.

We'll also prepare to castle by developing the bishop to c4.

r1b1k2r/ppppnppp/2n3q1/2b5/2BNP3/2P1B3/P.text:
This is the least popular move, played in less than 10% of the games. 

Black targets e4 and g2.

We'll trade on c6.

r1b1k2r/ppppnppp/3q4/4n2B/1P1B4/2P5/P2N1.text: The rook will be very potent on e1, as Black's king is still in the center and there is now an immediate attack on the e5-knight.

r1b1k2r/ppppnppp/5q2/2b1n3/2BNP3/2P1B3/P.text:
In 20% of the games, Black attacks the bishop on c4 by playing ...Ne5.

We'll retreat our bishop to e2, taking away squares from the knight on e5.

The idea is to play f4 without allowing ...Ng4.

r1b1k2r/ppppnppp/6q1/2b1n3/3N4/2P1B3/PP1.text:
Black must move the queen yet again.

Let's gain yet another tempo on the queen!

r1b1k2r/ppppnppp/6q1/2b1n3/3NP3/2P1B3/PP.text:
Black attacks both the e4 and g2-pawns.

This occured in 30% of the games.

We'll castle and protect g2.

r1b1k2r/ppppnppp/8/2b1n2B/3N4/2PqB3/PP1N.text:
Black tries to be annoying by keeping their queen in our camp.

This happens in almost 60% of the games!

r1b1k2r/ppppnppp/8/2b1n2B/8/2PqBN2/PP1N1.text:
We offer to trade the knights. 

After ....Nxf3+ Qxf3 and our position is great, with better development than Black.

...Bxe3 Nxe5 ...Qxd2 Bxf7+ and White is once again much better.

r1b1k2r/ppppnppp/8/2b1n3/3Nq3/2P1B3/PP2B.text:
We lose a pawn but in return, our pieces will get rapid development.

We'll start with Nd2, when the queen is attacked.

r1b2rk1/1pppnppp/1p6/4P3/2B5/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
c4 is a great square for the bishop: it aims at Black's king while also covering the a2-pawn.

We'll continue by advancing on the kingside with g3-f4 and centralizing the h1-rook.

r1b2rk1/1pppnppp/1p6/4P3/8/2N5/PPP2PPP/2.text: Black's king gets out of the center.

r1b2rk1/p1ppnppp/1p6/2q5/2B1P3/2P5/PP1Q1.text: If you compare the bishops, our bishop on c4 is much more active.

r1b2rk1/p1ppnppp/1p6/2q5/2B1P3/N1P5/PP1Q.text:
We finish our development by protecting the bishop on c4 and connecting the rooks. 

We will also centralize our rooks to gain greater control of the center.

r1b2rk1/p1ppnppp/1pn2q2/2b5/2BNP3/2P1B3/.text:
Very few games continue with ...b6.

Now Qd2 prepares to connect the rooks and supports the bishop on e3.

r1b2rk1/p1ppnppp/1pn3q1/2b5/2BNP3/2P1B3/.text:
Black decides to attack the pawn on e4 directly.

We'll trade on c6, intending to trade off Black's powerful dark-squared bishop next.

r1b2rk1/p1ppnppp/1pq5/2b5/2B1P3/2P1B3/PP.text:
Black recaptures with the queen.

We'll take on c5 as planned.

r1b2rk1/pp2nppp/3Q1q2/2B1n3/4p3/2P5/PP2B.text:
We've got the pawn back!

We'll have control over the e-file, plus we are attacking e7 and threatening to damage Black's pawn structure with Qxf6.

r1b2rk1/ppp1nppp/2np1q2/2b5/2BNP3/2P1B3/.text:
In a quarter of the games, Black opens up the light-squared bishop with ...d6. 

Moves like ...Bb6 or ...a6 don't really accomplish anything.

The pressure against our knight on d4 hinders our development slightly, so we'll remove it by trading on c6.

r1b2rk1/ppp1nppp/3b1q2/1NB1n3/4p3/2P5/PP.text:
Black must get their king out of the center now.

We'll regain the material by trading on d6.

r1b2rk1/ppp1nppp/3p1q2/2b1n3/3NPP2/2P1B3.text: And now we gain space on the kingside with f4, with the plans of expanding with b4 and finishing the development.

r1b2rk1/ppp2ppp/2n2q2/2p5/2B1P3/2P5/PP3P.text:
Black recaptures.

We'll gain some space in the center by pushing f4.

r1b2rk1/ppp2ppp/2np1q2/2b5/2B1P3/2P1B3/P.text:
Blacks keeps their structure intact and recaptures with the knight.

Now we'll trade off the dark-squared bishop.

It was Black's most active piece, and this trade also doubles Black's c-pawns.

r1b2rk1/ppppnppp/2n2q2/2b5/2BNP3/2P1B3/P.text:
Nearly 40% of the time Black castles here. 

It's the most natural move in this position.

We'll get the king into safety as well. 

Ideally, we want to trade off some of Black's most active pieces.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b5/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP.text:
This is the second most popular continuation, occurring in 24% of the games. 

Black adds an attacker to our knight on d4.

We'll support our strong piece on d4 by bringing the bishop out to e3.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/8/2b5/3nP3/4B3/PPP2PPP.text:
In 10% of the games, Black traded the knights on d4.

We'll recapture with the bishop.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/8/8/3bP3/8/PPP2PPP/RN1.text:
Our bishop aimed at the weak g7-pawn, so Black trades also trades the bishops.

We recapture. 

Our queen is nicely centralized now, and Black cannot attack it with any of their minor pieces.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
Black develops in the same manner.

And now, after striking in the center with 3.d4, the Scotch is on the board.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
70% of the time, Black trades on d4.

We'll recapture.

r3k2r/pppbnppp/2np1q2/2b5/2BNP3/2P1B3/PP.text:
Black intends to castle queenside.

We'll play Qd2, connecting the rooks and continuing to support the knight on d4.

r4rk1/pbppnppp/1pn2q2/2b5/2BNP3/2P1B3/PP.text:
Black fianchettoes.

This places indirect pressure on the e4-pawn.

r4rk1/pbppnppp/1pn2q2/2b5/2BNPP2/2P1B3/P.text:
And here comes the classic f4-move, gaining some space on the kingside. 

Ideas of e5 and b4 are still present!

r4rk1/ppp1qppp/2n1b3/2p1P3/2B2P2/2P5/PP4.text:
Black retreats the queen.

We'll trade off the bishops, as retreating would be too passive.

r4rk1/ppp2ppp/2n1bq2/2p5/2B1PP2/2P5/PP4P.text:
Black offers to trade the light-squared bishops.

We push forward, creating a threat against Black's queen.

r4rk1/ppp2ppp/2n1q3/2p1P3/5P2/2P5/PP4PP/.text:
Black recaptures with the queen.

Our knight comes to d2, where it will either jump to e4 or f3.

Both squares are suitable in this position.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black responds with ...e5.

We'll bring out the knight to its natural square in e4, e5 openings.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In this study, we'll take a look at Black's fourth move — 4...Bc5. 

Black attacks d4 with the bishop, which occurs in 24% of the games.

Let's check it out, starting with 1.e4!

1r1q1rk1/p1pn1ppp/3bb3/3B4/8/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
And we develop the knight to c3 and support our strong bishop on d5.

We are up a pawn and Black's queenside pawns are looking weak!

1r1q1rk1/p1pn1ppp/3bb3/3B4/8/8/PPP2PPP/R.text: Black gets the king out of the center.

1r1qk2r/p1pn1ppp/2Bbb3/3p4/8/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Black must move the rook.

And now we can win a pawn and increase the pressure on the e6-bishop.

1r1qk2r/p1pnbppp/2B1b3/3p4/8/2N5/PPP1QPP.text:
...we develop the knight and soon the d5-pawn will fall.

For example, 13...0-0 and we will capture with 14.Bxd5. We ideally want to take with the bishop so that our pressure on the e-file is felt a lot more.

r1b1k2r/p1ppqppp/2p2n2/2b1P3/8/3B4/PPP2P.text:
Black pins our pawn to the knight with the queen.

We can see this in around 40% of the games.

So, naturally, we'll castle, getting the king away from the pin.

Black of course cannot grab the pawn on e5, because of the Re1 pin.

r1b1k2r/p1ppqppp/2p5/2bnP3/8/3B4/PPP2PPP.text:
Black moves the knight.

We'll develop our knight. It will sit nicely on the e4-square.

r1b2qk1/p1p2p1p/2pp2p1/2bnP3/4Q3/3B4/PPP.text:
The queen is nicely centralized on e4. We'll finish our development and enjoy the material advantage!

Nd2 and Re1 are good, improving moves. 

If 12...Bf5, 13.Qa4 attacks c6 and we have a great position.

r1b2qk1/p1p2p1p/2pp2p1/2bnP3/6Q1/3B4/PPP.text: Black opens up an attack on our queen.

r1b2qk1/p1pp1p1p/2p3p1/2bnP3/6Q1/3B4/PPP.text:
Black recaptures.

Now it's time to get our king into safety.

r1b2r2/p1ppqp1k/1bp2p2/4P3/1nP3Q1/8/PP3P.text:
The king moves.

Another check, this time on h4! 

Now the dark-squared bishop will come in handy.

r1b2r2/p1ppqp1k/1bp2p2/4P3/1nP5/8/PP3PPP.text:
Black captures.

Now we bring the queen into the attack with check.

Black's pawns prevent the king running away and limit the defensive scope of their queen!

r1b2rk1/p1pp1p2/1bp2p1B/4q3/1nP4Q/8/PP3P.text:
This is Black's only resource not to get checkmated immediately.

We still have the check on g4.

r1b2rk1/p1pp1p2/1bp2p1B/6q1/1nP3Q1/8/PP3.text: Black must cover with the queen, otherwise Qg7 is checkmate.

r1b2rk1/p1pp1p2/1bp2p2/6B1/1nP3Q1/8/PP3P.text: But now we win the queen.

r1b2rk1/p1ppqp1p/1bp2p2/4P3/1nP5/3B4/PP3.text:
Black grabs the material.

And here comes another sacrifice!

r1b2rk1/p1ppqp2/1bp2p2/4P2Q/1nP5/8/PP3PP.text:
Black moves to g8.

Check again! 

All of our moves should come with a check or a checkmate threat, so that Black does not have time to mobilize their defense.

r1b2rk1/p1ppqp2/1bp2p2/4P3/1nP4Q/8/PP3PP.text:
The king moves to g8.

Now we threaten a checkmate in two. Black can't prevent the coming check on the g-file.

r1b2rk1/p1ppqppp/1bp5/3nP3/4N3/3B4/PPP2P.text:
...so Black retreats.

With c4, we'll gain more space on the queenside and get rid of Black's strong knight on d5.

r1b2rk1/p1ppqppp/1bp5/4P3/1nP1N3/3B4/PP3.text:
Black puts pressure on our bishop.

Their pieces aren't developed well, meanwhile, all of our pieces aim at Black's kingside! 

This calls for a sacrifice.

Now Nf6+ is a very powerful move.

r1b2rk1/p1ppqppp/2p5/2bnP3/8/3B4/PPPN1PP.text:
Black gets the king into safety.

We can try to win the bishop pair while centralizing our knight...

r1bq1rk1/p1p1bppp/5n2/3p4/8/1P1B4/P1P2PP.text:
Black castles. 

Now we'll play Bb2, with control along the long diagonal.

r1bq1rk1/p1pp1p1p/2p3pB/2bnP3/6Q1/3B4/PP.text:
This is the only move to defend and avoid major material losses.

We can grab the rook now and be an exchange up.

r1bq1rk1/p1pp1ppp/2p5/2bnP3/6Q1/3B4/PPP2.text:
Black castles to defend the g7-pawn. 

Other moves are passive.

Now Bh6 threatens a checkmate! 

Black of course cannot capture the bishop: it is pinned due to the good placement of our queen.

r1bq1rk1/p3bppp/5n2/2pp4/8/1P1B3P/PBP2PP.text:
We will now continue our development with moves like Re1 and Nd2. 

Bf1 can be played if we need it to put our bishop on a safe square and defend our kingside. This is an equal position, but our moves are easy to find. 

Black can make a strategic mistake with ...d4, giving us the c4-square as an outpost for a piece.

r1bq1rk1/p3bppp/5n2/2pp4/8/1P1B4/PBP2PPP.text:
The pawn duo in the center for Black appears to be advantageous, but the position is equal. 

With h3, we ensure that Black won't get access to g4.

r1bqk2r/p1p1bppp/5n2/3p4/8/3B4/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Black prepares to castle with ...Be7, occurring in almost 70% of the games.

Our fianchetto on b2 will prove valuable against Black's kingside.

Black retreats the bishop to e7, essentially losing a tempo.

We'll create a queen-rook battery aimed at the dark-squared bishop, so that Black cannot castle immediately.

r1bqk2r/p1p2p1p/2pp2pB/2bnP3/6Q1/3B4/PPP.text:
...d6 opens up an attack on our queen.

We'll shift the queen to the queenside, attacking the c6-pawn.

r1bqk2r/p1p2ppp/3b1n2/3p4/8/3B4/PPP2PPP/.text:
Black develops the bishop to d6, which is the second most popular move after ...Be7.

We can improve our rook with a check.

r1bqk2r/p1pp1p1p/2p3p1/2bnP3/6Q1/3B4/PPP.text:
This is the top move in the database, played 40% of the time.

It defends g7, but creates some dark-squared weaknesses.

We'll exploit them by placing our bishop on h6, preventing Black from castling.

r1bqk2r/p1pp1ppp/2p2n2/2b5/4P3/3B4/PPP2P.text:
Black brings the bishop to c5, eyeing the f2-pawn. 

This move is not the strongest one, yet it is played 30% of the time.

We will push e5 here, kicking the knight away from its natural square and opening up our light-squared bishop.

r1bqk2r/p1pp1ppp/2p5/2bnP3/8/3B4/PPP2PPP.text:
Black jumps to d5, the only logical square for the knight.

g4 is a great square for our queen now. 

It attacks the undefended g7-pawn and will pose some danger to Black if they castle kingside.

r1bqkb1r/p1p2ppp/2p2n2/3p4/4P3/3B4/PPP2P.text:
This is the most popular, and also the strongest move Black could go for, played in more than half of the games. 

Black immediately challenges our central pawn on e4.

We'll trade here, getting rid of the pressure and opening our light-squared bishop.

r1bqkb1r/p1p2ppp/5n2/3p4/8/3B4/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Black recaptures with the pawn.

We'll get the king into safety and potentially the rook into action on the e-file.

r1bqkb1r/p1pp1ppp/2p2n2/8/4P3/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
Black's pawns are doubled...

...and now we'll develop with Bd3, supporting the pawn on e4 and preparing to castle.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP.text:
And Black develops the knight to f6, eyeing our e4-pawn.

At the club level, this is the third most popular move, but in the Masters database, it's the most played one.

This is the engine's top choice.

We'll trade off the knights.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
Black defends their e-pawn.

With d4, our opening is now on the board! The Scotch.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
Black trades in the center.

We'll recapture with the knight.

r2qk2r/p1p1bppp/4bn2/3p4/8/3B4/PPP1QPPP/.text:
Black blocks the e-file.

Now we'll give a check on b5, making use of the light squares yet again.

r2qk2r/p1p2ppp/3bbn2/3p4/8/3B4/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Black blocks the check with the light-squared bishop.

Now that Black's light-squared bishop has abandoned its home square (and is pinned), we'll give a check on b5.

r2qk2r/p1pb1p1p/2p3pB/2bnp3/Q7/3B4/PPP2P.text: Black closes the e-file by capturing on e5.

r2qk2r/p1pb1p1p/2pp2pB/2bnP3/Q7/3B4/PPP2.text:
Black defends it.

We'll get the king into safety and prepare to activate the rook.

r2qk2r/p1pb1pBp/2p3p1/2bnp3/Q7/3B4/PPP2P.text:
But now we get a strong hold of the center and quick development with Black's castling nonexistent!

We will win a pawn and then it's up to us to consolidate by developing our pieces with moves like Nc3 and Re1, and holding on to the pawn advantage.

r2qk2r/p1pn1ppp/3bb3/1B1p4/8/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Black's only reasonable move is to cover the check with the knight.

Now we'll attack both the d5-pawn and the rook on a8.

r2qk2r/p1pnbppp/4b3/1B1p4/8/8/PPP1QPPP/R.text:
Black blocks the check.

We'll attack the rook and put pressure on the d5-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black copies us.

We'll develop, attacking e5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the third Study of the Scotch! 

In the previous chapter we covered 4...Bc5, but now we're going to take a look at the engine's top choice at the fourth move which is 4...Nf6, attacking our pawn on e4.

Let's dive into it, starting with 1.e4!

N1bk1bnr/pp1p1ppp/8/4n3/8/2P2B1q/PP3P1P/.text:
Sure, Black could continue the aggression with ...Ne5, attacking our bishop.

But they are playing with the only two pieces they have activated in the opening.

N1bk1bnr/pp1p1ppp/8/4n3/8/2P4q/PP2BP1P/R.text:
We will just retreat and enjoy a winning position.

Black has no more threats and we want to centralize the queen on d5 and play Bf4 to attack the knight and take the diagonal.

It's not even going to be easy for Black to win our knight on a8.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/1N6/4q3/2b5/PPP1BP.text:
Black takes on c3.

We don't want to recapture with the knight and allow them to capture on g2.

That would be bad for us. Instead, we'll take with the pawn and maintain the threat to c7.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/1b1NP2q/2N5/PPP2.text:
And that's to pin our defender. Now the threat on the knight is reintroduced.

We don't want to complicate things by playing Nxc6, allowing Qe4+.

In fact, the best move is to actually develop and pre-emptively block the incoming capture so that it no longer arrives with check.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/1b1Nq3/2N5/PPP1B.text:
They can take the pawn here, but this is actually better for White.

The queen leaving its post early has left the c7-pawn unattended.

So we'll jump to b5 and attack the c7-pawn. It's actually not that easy to defend.

r1b1kbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/3q4/3N4/8/PPP1QPPP/.text:
But we don't have to play by their rules and permit a queen trade.

The best move for Black is to block with the bishop on e6 and allow us to capture it.

Otherwise, if they block with the bishop or the knight on e7, White is already winning after Nb5, when the queen would have to retreat passively to defend c7.

r1b1kbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/3q4/3N4/8/PPP2PPP/R.text: Sure, Black can activate their queen and attack the knight...

r1b1kbnr/pppp1ppp/2n2q2/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP.text:
The move ...Qf6 is probably positionally the best sideline.

It's played 5% of the time, which is still almost 2.5 million games!

Black is attacking our knight once again and often wants to slide to g6 to keep the queen active.

We'll protect the knight for now, with c3.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1ppp/2n3q1/8/3NP3/2P5/PP3PP.text:
Capturing on d4 would be a mistake, giving us strong central pawns. Instead, a logical move is to move to g6, attacking e4, and freeing f6 for the knight.

What they might not know is that we can let them capture the pawn!

Because the queen has come out early, Nb5 is an extremely potent move, targeting the pawn on c7 and threatening a fork.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/1N6/4q3/2P5/PP3PPP.text:
Even if Black captures on e4...

It just gives us more room to develop, while blocking the check.

You might notice that this move sacrifices the g2-pawn as well.

Well, this double sacrifice is actually the way to go for White.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/1N6/8/2P2B1q/PP3P1.text:
The queen has to escape to a square like h3...

After which we can fork Black with the capture on c7.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/1N6/8/2P5/PP2BPqP/.text:
Because White is winning if Black takes this pawn.

We can defend our rook with Bf3, also attacking the black queen, and the fork on c7 is still a problem for Black.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/3NP2q/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
The move ...Qh4 is played only 2% of the time, but does have some merit to it.

In fact, Black has a bigger win rate than White in this line in the database.

The queen attacks the e4-pawn.

We can defend it with the knight, but Black has an answer to that too.

r1bk1bnr/ppNp1ppp/2n5/8/8/2P2B1q/PP3P1P/.text:
And once the king moves...

We'll grab the rook.

A good trade for two pawns.

r1bk2nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/1N6/4q3/2P5/P1P1BPP.text:
In that case, we will just castle, and let's take a look at what we got in this position.

We are down a pawn, but we've acquired the bishop pair.

Apart from that, we have more space to develop and a lead in activity, while Black has lost their castling rights.

White is better here.

Now Black basically has to side-step to d8 and protect the pawn.

Other than that, there aren't many good moves.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/3p4/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
The move ...d5 is only played 1% of the time, and it doesn't accomplish much for Black.

We will take on d5 and release the unnecessary tension in the center.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
And Black defends it.

With d4 we reach the Scotch Game.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
Black takes on d4.

And we will recapture.

All this we've seen before.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black responds with ...e5.

The knight gets out and attacks the central pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In Chapter 4 of our course on the Scotch, we will take a look at some sidelines on move 4 for Black, namely moving the queen to either f6 or h4, as well as striking in the center early with ...d5.

Moving the queen is premature but can be dangerous, so we have to know how to respond.

 Let's begin with 1.e4.

r1bk1bnr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/4p3/2N5/PPP2PPP/R.text: And after developing the knight we'll target the e4-pawn, bring the bishops to c4 and g5 and enjoy our castling rights!

r1bq1b1r/ppp2kpp/2np4/4P3/4n3/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
Black recaptures.

Our queen now arrives on d5 with check, forking the king and the e4-knight.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1P3/2B1n3/5N2/PPP.text:
Black piles up on the f2-square.

But f7 is also a target. With Qd5, we continue with our plan, and a checkmate is now threatened!

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/3QP3/2B1n3/5N2/PPP1.text: ...but after Ke2, Black's positions falls apart, since they cannot defend both of their pieces and a checkmate threat on f7 at the same time.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/3QP3/2B1n3/5N2/PPP2.text: Black captures on f2 with a check...

r1bqkb1r/ppp1nppp/3p1n2/3Pp3/2P1P3/5N2/P.text:
Black brings out the knight with an attack on the e4-pawn.

We'll develop. c3 is a natural square for the knight.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2np4/4P3/2B1n3/5N2/PPP2.text:
Black offers another pawn for a quick development. ...d6 is the fourth most popular move.

Now we can sacrifice our bishop on f7.

The motif of bringing our queen to d5 is apparent yet again!

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP.text:
Black develops the knight, counter-attacking our pawn on e4.

This is the third most popular move, occurring 7% of the time, representing over 1 million games!

We'll win a pawn on e5 and attack the knight.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/4P3/4n3/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
Black regains the pawn.

Now c4 is a great square for our light-squared bishop. 

We immediately start to eye the weak f7-pawn. There are ideas of bringing the queen to d5 and threatening checkmate!

r1bqkbnr/ppp1nppp/3p4/3Pp3/4P3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
Back retreats to e7 instead of jumping straight back to b8.

If instead ...Nb4, we have a3, and after ...Na6 then Bxa6 when we have seriously damaged Black's pawn structure.

After Nce7 we'll add to our pawn center with c4.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/3pp3/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
Black goes for a central counter-attack with 3...d5. This move occurs very rarely.

We can grab the pawn on e5, getting our knight to a strong square at the same time.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4N3/3Pp3/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
Black continues with the second most popular move which is grabbing the pawn on e4.

We'll put pressure on the c6-knight by pinning it.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2np4/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
This move is played only 10% of the time, but it is the second most popular move! 

Black's idea is to support the e5-pawn and avoid opening up the center.

We can now gain space in the center with a tempo on Black's c6-knight.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3pn3/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Black trades, which happens in 60% of the time.

We'll recapture the knight.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/4p3/8/PPP2PPP/RNB.text:
Black must regain the pawn, or they'll just be a pawn down without any real compensation.

Trading the queens is good for us here, since Black will lose their castling rights in an otherwise symmetrical position.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
Black develops the knight and supports e5.

Now 3.d4 is the Scotch!

r2q1b1r/ppp1k1pp/2n1b3/4p1N1/4Q3/8/PPP2P.text:
Blacks moves the king and must also guard the e6-bishop.

We'll grab the bishop, luring Black's king into the open.

r2q1b1r/ppp2kpp/2n1b3/4p3/4Q3/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
Black recaptures on e5 with the pawn to free up their pieces and go for some activity. 8...Be7 was also possible.

But their king isn't safe! 

We must keep attacking here, or Black will escape. Thus we'll play Ng5+.

r2q1b1r/ppp2kpp/2npb3/3QP3/4n3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
Black attacks our queen and blocks the check.

We'll regain the piece.

r2q1b1r/ppp3pp/2n1k3/4p3/4Q3/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
We can just develop here. 

Black's king is feeling very exposed and our knight will most likely end up on the d5-square. 

We can choose to castle either side, depending on Black's plan of hiding their king!

r2q1rk1/ppp1bpp1/3p1nn1/3Pp1Bp/2P1P2P/2N.text:
After Bg5 we can plan to capture the knight on f6 and grab the pawn on h5 next.

White is doing very well here, as we have a space advantage on the kingside, and our pieces are better placed than Black's.

r2q1rk1/ppp1bpp1/3p1nn1/3Pp2p/2P1P2P/2N2.text: Black gets their king into safety.

r2qk2r/ppp1bpp1/3p1nn1/3Pp2p/2P1P2P/2N2Q.text:
Black prepares to castle.

Black is without a light-squared bishop, so our own bishop is a very powerful piece! We'll activate it on h3.

r2qkb1r/pp2nppp/2pp1nb1/3Pp3/2P1P1P1/2NB.text: Black tries to undermine our pawn chain.

But we can simply bring yet another piece to a better square. 

Black's pieces are looking very cramped on the kingside since we have a space advantage there.

Our plan can revolve around gaining further space there and hiding our king on the queenside.

r2qkb1r/ppp1nppp/3p1n2/3Pp2b/2P1P3/2N2N1.text:
Black retreats to h5 to keep the pin.

We'll expand on the kingside and gain time on the bishop.

r2qkb1r/ppp1nppp/3p1n2/3Pp3/2P1P1b1/2N2N.text:
Black develops the bishop to g4, pinning our knight on f3.

We'll ask the bishop a question with h3.

r2qkb1r/ppp1nppp/3p1n2/3Pp3/2P1P3/2N2b1P.text:
Instead of retreating, Black immediately captures the knight on f3 which happens in around 50% of the games.

We should recapture with the queen to keep our pawn structure intact.

r2qkb1r/ppp1nppp/3p1nb1/3Pp3/2P1P1P1/2N2.text:
They retreat to g6.

Now we develop a piece with Bd3 and support the pawn on e4.

r2qkb1r/ppp2pp1/3p1nn1/3Pp2p/2P1P2P/2N2Q.text:
Black stops our intended advance.

Now g3 acomplishes three things:

supports the pawn on h4, protects the f4-square and allows for our light-squared bishop to be developed.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1nn1/3Pp3/2P1P3/2N2Q1P.text:
Black improves the knight and opens up e7 for the bishop.

Against a knight on g6, the h4 push is usually very powerful! 

We are threatening to push even further with h5, attacking the knight on g6.

r2qkbnr/pppb1ppp/2n5/1B2N3/3Pp3/8/PPP2PP.text:
Black defends it with the bishop.

As Black was threatening to capture the knight on e5, we'll get rid of the bishop and keep the knight on c6 pinned!

r3kbnr/pppq1ppp/2n5/1B6/3Pp3/2P5/PP3PPP/.text: And with c3 we support the pawn on d4 while preparing to target the e4-pawn by developing and castling kingside. The c6-knight remains pinned.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black responds symmetrically.

We'll develop the knight, attacking e5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Hello and welcome to the fifth chapter!

In the last chapter, Black deviated on the fourth move, since they've still continued to trade on d4. 

In this study, we'll check out some of Black's moves that avoid capturing on d4.

We'll begin with 1.e4.
